answer.rationale: Three concurrent signals: latency spike confined to primary region, release deployed 2 hours ago, and settlement traffic at peak. The release timing (90 min degradation starting ~30 min post-release) strongly suggests the release is the root cause, consistent with memory_b1 (rollback cleared checkout error spike) and memory_b2 (regional failover restored latency fast). I verify both because the intervention space splits into two plausible candidates. memory_b1 confirms that rollback is safe and effective when a release causes a degradation; memory_b2 confirms that regional failover is fast but does not address the underlying bad build. Since the degradation is confined to the primary region AND a release just went out, rollback removes the root cause everywhere rather than shifting traffic onto a still-bad build in the secondary region. Rolling back preserves customer writes (the prior build was stable per memory_b1), avoids capacity contention during settlement peak, and resolves the issue at its source. Regional failover would be the fallback if rollback itself stalls, but given one intervention, rollback is the higher-leverage move. The 2-hour release window is still fresh enough for a clean rollback; the 90-minute latency climb has not yet produced write failures, only degradation, so acting now prevents data loss.
